reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Scriver's OMMBID
clinicalPearls: Caused by deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme alpha-N-acetylgalactosaminidase, leading to accumulation of glycopeptides and glycolipids with terminal N-acetylgalactosamine
Type I is a severe infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy with developmental regression, seizures, and cortical visual impairment
Type II (Kanzaki disease) is a milder adult-onset form with angiokeratoma corporis diffusum and mild cognitive changes
Intermediate phenotypes between the two extremes are also recognised
Angiokeratomas in the adult form can mimic those seen in Fabry disease, an important distinguishing point
Urinary oligosaccharide and glycopeptide screening supports the diagnosis
Confirmation rests on deficient alpha-N-acetylgalactosaminidase activity and NAGA gene testing
reference.pathophysiology: Schindler disease is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in NAGA, encoding lysosomal alpha-N-acetylgalactosaminidase. This enzyme removes terminal alpha-N-acetylgalactosamine residues from glycoproteins, glycopeptides, and glycolipids during lysosomal degradation. Its deficiency leads to accumulation of these incompletely degraded compounds and their excretion in the urine. The mechanism linking substrate storage to the severe infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy of type I remains incompletely understood, but the phenotype features widespread axonal swellings (spheroids). Type II (Kanzaki disease) presents in adulthood with cutaneous angiokeratomas and only mild neurological involvement, and intermediate presentations occur. Inheritance is autosomal recessive.
additionalDifferentials: Fabry disease, given overlapping angiokeratoma corporis diffusum in the adult form
Infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy from other causes (e.g. PLA2G6-related)
Other oligosaccharidoses such as fucosidosis and alpha-mannosidosis
Other causes of early developmental regression with seizures
additionalInvestigations: Leucocyte or fibroblast alpha-N-acetylgalactosaminidase enzyme assay
Skin biopsy of angiokeratomas in the adult form
Neurophysiology and developmental assessment where regression is present
redFlags: Progressive developmental regression with seizures in infancy
Loss of previously acquired motor and cognitive skills
New angiokeratomas prompting distinction from Fabry disease
reference.prognosis: The infantile type I form is severe with profound neurological deterioration and a poor outlook, whereas the adult type II form follows a much milder course compatible with long survival. No disease-modifying therapy is established.
pitfalls: Confusing the adult angiokeratoma phenotype with Fabry disease without appropriate enzyme testing
Overlooking the diagnosis in infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy without metabolic screening
Relying only on glycosaminoglycan screening and missing the oligosaccharide pattern
Assuming a single uniform phenotype given the wide clinical spectrum
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
management: No disease-modifying therapy such as enzyme replacement or substrate reduction is established, so management is supportive and tailored to phenotype
In the infantile type I form, control seizures with antiseizure medication, provide feeding support, and treat spasticity and the consequences of neurodevelopmental regression
Support cortical visual impairment with physiotherapy and occupational therapy, and introduce palliative care planning in the severe infantile form
In adult type II (Kanzaki) disease, reassure and manage cutaneous angiokeratomas conservatively, using laser therapy for cosmetically troublesome lesions
Distinguish from Fabry disease, whose angiokeratomas overlap, to avoid inappropriate Fabry-directed enzyme therapy
Coordinate multidisciplinary care through metabolic medicine, neurology, dermatology and developmental services
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive NAGA disorder and screen at-risk family members
